summary: Over two iterations, score improved from 88.78 to 95.35 on the 2D rectangular knapsack problem (out of 100). The biggest gain (+6 points) came from always trying both item orientations; smaller gains came from a contact-point placement heuristic, bin transposition, and ordering local search. Roughly 5 points remain on the table, likely from geometric fragmentation on hard test cases with near-prime bin dimensions.
key_points: Iter-1 baseline: 88.78 (MaxRects with BL/BSSF/BAF heuristics, single orientation fallback, randomized search). Iter-2 result: 95.35 (both-orientation best-fit, contact-point heuristic, bin transposition, pairwise-swap local search, free-rect cap at 500).

Critical lesson: overhead management matters as much as algorithmic quality — adding a gap-fill phase that is individually helpful dropped the score from 95 to 89 by starving the random search of time within the 1-second budget.

Still unknown: (1) which of the 15 test cases contribute most to the remaining ~5% gap, (2) whether a fundamentally different approach (e.g., guillotine cutting, LP-guided type selection, or skyline packing) could break through the current ceiling.

Next iteration should investigate: (a) LP relaxation to bound per-type item counts before packing, reducing the ordering search space; (b) a skyline/shelf hybrid packer as an alternative geometry engine; (c) smarter time allocation — detect easy cases early and reallocate budget to harder ones; (d) finer-grained random search strategies (e.g., biased sampling toward high-density types rather than uniform shuffles).
